paragraph.text: B13. "A lobster boiled alive feels nothing and tastes fresher"

there is serious evidence that decapod crustaceans, such as lobsters and crabs, feel pain. A review of more than 300 studies led the United Kingdom to recognize them as sentient in 2022, and Switzerland has required since 2018 that they be stunned before being killed and banned transporting them alive on ice. Boiling the animal alive is choosing the slowest way to kill it for the sake of freshness. Stunning reduces suffering at the moment of death, but it doesn't solve the main problem: killing an animal who can feel, without need, is still unjust.
"Lobster has to be boiled alive, it's fresher. And it doesn't feel anything, it's basically a sea insect."
Crustaceans have a much simpler nervous system than mammals.
Without a complex nervous system, there is no pain.

P1 is true. P2 is the premise in dispute, and the evidence points against it. P3 has some truth about freshness, but it doesn't require boiling a conscious animal.
"It has to be boiled alive or it goes off."
"The noise in the pot is just air escaping the shell."
"Crustaceans have no cortex, so they don't process pain."
"Fish and invertebrates don't feel pain." (which is A2)

Lobsters and crabs move and try to escape when they're put into hot water. Scientists studied them and found that they probably feel pain. That's why some countries require them to be knocked out first, instead of being boiled alive. That makes it hurt less, but the animal still loses its life.

The evidence indicates that lobsters and crabs feel pain: a review of more than 300 studies led the United Kingdom to recognize them as sentient in 2022. Switzerland has required since 2018 that they be stunned before being killed and banned transporting them alive on ice. Boiling the animal alive is choosing the slowest way to kill it, and freshness doesn't depend on it. And stunning first reduces suffering, but it doesn't make killing it just.
"If the lobster feels nothing, why does it try to escape the pot?"

text.bold: 1. The evidence of pain is serious.

paragraph.text: The review commissioned by the UK government from the London School of Economics assessed more than 300 studies and concluded there is strong evidence of sentience in decapod crustaceans and cephalopods. On that basis, the UK's 2022 animal sentience law included these animals (A2).

text.bold: 2. Countries have already changed the rules.

paragraph.text: Switzerland, since March 2018, requires lobsters to be stunned before being killed, by electric shock or mechanical destruction of the brain, and banned transporting them on ice. It's progress, because it reduces suffering at the moment of death. But the rule still treats the essential point as normal: killing, without need, an animal for whom there is serious evidence of feeling. A less painful death is still an imposed death, and stunning answers the how, not the whether (B1).
Stunning immediately before cooking keeps the freshness. The tradition of boiling alive is habit, not necessity.
Even for those who still have doubts, the cost of being wrong is high: if the animal feels, it goes through a slow and painful death.
Review of more than 300 studies: strong evidence of sentience in decapod crustaceans and cephalopods

It's true that crustaceans are very different from us, that there is still scientific debate about their experience, and that freshness matters for food safety.

But the latest evidence led governments to protect them, and freshness doesn't require boiling the animal alive. When in doubt, care is the reasonable choice, and the next question is whether it needs to be killed at all.
